proposal: As part of Navarro's China package, the chapter recommends prohibiting Chinese investment in high-technology industries, barring U.S. pension funds from holding Chinese stocks, delisting Chinese companies that do not meet PCAOB audit standards (or closing the A-shares market to U.S. investment and deregistering sanctioned firms), barring Hong Kong clearinghouses as transit points for capital going to the mainland, and keeping Chinese sovereign bonds out of U.S. investors' portfolios.

source_checks.note: Memorandum of 2025-02-21 directs CFIUS and other tools against PRC-affiliated investment in strategic sectors, a review of outbound limits (including publicly traded securities and pension fund investment), updated ERISA fiduciary standards so foreign adversary companies are ineligible for plan contributions, and reviews of HFCAA audit standards and VIE structures; it does not direct delisting.

EBSA proposed rule at 91 FR 16088, published 2026-03-31, comments closed 2026-06-01; it says only that fiduciaries may not select an otherwise illegal investment (example: a foreign adversary on the OFAC SDN list) and does not mention China or bar any country's stocks.

SEC order dated 2026-05-14, published 2026-05-19 (91 FR 29183), grants accelerated approval to Nasdaq's China listing criteria: at least $25 million in U.S. firm-commitment proceeds or unrestricted public float, no direct listings on two tiers, one-year seasoning for transfers; applies to initial listings, delists no one, and adds no PCAOB inspection test.

significance.rationale: Barring pension funds from Chinese stocks and delisting firms affects US investors and capital flows to China.

status_summary: The administration has acted on parts of this package through a memorandum, a statute and an exchange rule, but not through the prohibitions the chapter lists. The America First Investment Policy memorandum (2025-02-21) directs tools including CFIUS to restrict PRC-affiliated investment in technology, critical infrastructure and other strategic sectors, orders a review of expanded limits on U.S. outbound investment in sectors such as semiconductors, AI and quantum, directs fiduciary standards under ERISA aimed at making foreign adversary companies ineligible for pension plan contributions, and directs a review of audit standards and variable interest entity structures for China-based issuers; it does not itself direct delisting. Congress codified and expanded the Outbound Investment Security Program in the FY2026 defense law (reported signed 2025-12-18), covering China, with Treasury regulations due within 450 days; its exceptions include certain publicly traded securities and limited partner interests, and the existing program stays in force until then. On pensions, a Labor Department proposal published 2026-03-31 says only that fiduciaries cannot select an otherwise illegal investment, such as one in a foreign adversary on the OFAC sanctions list; it does not restrict Chinese stocks generally, and no rule barring pension funds from holding them was found. On listings, the SEC approved on an accelerated basis (notice published 2026-05-19) a Nasdaq rule adding initial listing criteria for companies primarily operating in China, including at least $25 million in U.S. offering proceeds or unrestricted public float; it applies to new listings and does not delist existing companies. No delisting program, closure of the A-shares market, or limit on Hong Kong clearinghouses or Chinese sovereign bonds was found. On the inbound side, Treasury asked on 2026-02-09 for input on streamlining CFIUS review through a Known Investor Program, the May 2026 state visit chartered a Board of Investment, and a law-firm alert of 2026-09-24 reports that board stalled, with Beijing seeking a pre-cleared list of industries and Washington preferring case-by-case review.

timeline.event: America First Investment Policy memorandum directs CFIUS and other tools against PRC-affiliated investment in strategic sectors, a review of outbound investment limits, ERISA fiduciary standards on foreign adversary holdings, and a review of audit standards and variable interest entities for China-based issuers.
SEC publishes Nasdaq's proposed rule adding initial listing criteria for companies primarily operating in China.

The COINS Act, codifying and expanding the Outbound Investment Security Program (China including Hong Kong and Macau; semiconductors, quantum, AI, hypersonics, high-performance computing), is reported signed as Title LXXXV of the FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act; Treasury regulations are due within 450 days.
Treasury's Office of Investment Security requests public input on streamlining CFIUS review, including through a Known Investor Program.

Labor Department's Employee Benefits Security Administration proposes a rule on fiduciary duties in selecting plan investment options that says fiduciaries cannot choose an otherwise illegal investment, such as one in a foreign adversary on the OFAC sanctions list.
White House fact sheet on a state visit to China says a U.S.-China Board of Investment is chartered as a government-to-government forum on investment-related issues.
SEC publishes its order granting accelerated approval to Nasdaq's initial listing criteria for companies primarily operating in China (as modified by Amendment No. 3).

A law-firm alert reports that the Board of Investment remains stalled, with Beijing seeking a pre-cleared list of eligible industries and Washington preferring case-by-case review, and does not address outbound investment restrictions.

title: Limit Chinese investment, U.S. pension and portfolio flows to China, and Chinese listings
uncertainties: The signing date of the COINS Act (2025-12-18) comes from a Baker McKenzie post that does not give its own date; Covington's 2025-12-17 alert says only that the House had passed the bill, and the public law number was not found. The Nasdaq rule's contents were read from titles and short excerpts, so how strict the China criteria are is not stated. Federal Register searches on outbound investment, the Holding Foreign Companies Accountable Act and ERISA foreign adversary rules found no Treasury, SEC or Labor action matching the pension, delisting, clearinghouse or sovereign bond items, but absence of a Federal Register document does not rule out other action (for example PCAOB or sanctions steps). Hong Kong clearinghouses and Chinese sovereign bonds were not searched beyond those queries. Overlaps c26-02, which holds the overall decoupling assessment.
